=== H-E-B, LP and South Texas Electric Cooperative, Inc's Joint Comments on the PFP in Dkt. 58000.pdf ===
PROJECT NO. 58000

RULEMAKING TO UPDATE § PUBLIC UTILITY COMMISSION
WHOLESALE AND IOU RETAIL §

TRANSMISSION COST RECOVERY IN § OF TEXAS

THE ERCOT REGION §

H-E-B, LP AND SOUTH TEXAS ELECTRIC COOPERATIVE, INC.’S JOINT
COMMENTS ON THE PROPOSAL FOR PUBLICATION

H-E-B, LP (“H-E-B”) and South Texas Electric Cooperative, Inc. (“STEC”) respectfully
submit these Joint Comments on the Proposal for Publication (PFP) (the “Joint Comments”) issued
by the Public Utility Commission of Texas (“PUCT” or “Commission”) and to the Commission
Staff (“Staff”) questions included in the PFP. Comments must be filed by August 11, 2026; these

Joint Comments are timely filed.

L INTRODUCTION

In reviewing the PEP, it is clear that the key component missing is the review of the
assignment of costs for transmission investment. Senate Bill 6, Section 6(a) requires that the PUCT
evaluate whether the current four coincident peak (“4CP’”) appropriately assigns: costs. for
transmission investment. Based on the comments provided throughout Project No. 58484; there is
near consensus that the 4CP does not appropriately assign costs and that it is instead a mechanism
used by sophisticated large customers to avoid paying for the transmission they use and instead
shift those costs to other, smaller customer classes including residential and smal! commercial
customers, The comments in Project 58484 make clear that the current 4CP methodology used to
calculate wholesale transmission rates does not ensure that all loads appropriately contribute to the
recovery of an electric cooperative’s, electric utility’s or municipally-owned utility’s costs to

provide access to the transmission system, as required by Section 6(a)(1).

Significantly, the PFP uses a twelve CP (“12CP”) methodology, which is theoretically paid
by all existing customers in all customer classes, including the customers that have long avoided
payment under the 4CP methodology and will likely avoid payment under the 12CP methodology
in the same way, and without any guarantee of a minimum payment. The minimum billing demand
does not apply to loads unless they are both “new” and “large loads,” that is, above 75 MW. Asa

result, the PFP permits the gaming mechanism in effect for 4CP to be expanded over 12 months.

 There can be no cost assignment attributable to any CP, because CPs can always be avoided, and
result in other customers paying for the costs avoided by larger customers. The CP mechanism
itself is widely acknowledged as a gaming mechanism. Some loads have become quite adept at
avoiding these costs. What started as a small cottage industry has become big business in ERCOT.
This big business is canted in favor of large corporations with the ability to invest in sophisticated
forecasting systems or pay expensive consultants to tell them when to decrease load. They also
invest in equipment necessary to decrease that load. This makes economic sense for these loads
because it is cost-effective to invest in the systems, consultants and generation/batteries, to avoid

transmission charges year after year.

If the PFP were adopted as drafted, permitting CP avoidance to continue along its current
path, just with more months that need to be gamed, it will create additional reliability issues for
ERCOT. These loads will end their CP curtailments at the time the system is under its highest
stress, which is not when load is at its peak, but when the peak load period has ended and the
renewable ramp periods are on-going. These loads return to the system at precisely the wrong time
from a reliability perspective, and they will do so several times per month. The 12CP mechanism
will result in many more cycles of significant system load swings than under 4CP, which are limited
to chasing system peaks in each of the 4 summer months. 12CP will add 8 months during which
loads will be chasing the CP. That further erodes the energy-only market because loads will game
the system in more months, and decrease usage to avoid transmission costs, rather than in response
to generation costs—a problem that has been highlighted by the Independent Market Monitor for
many years. The PFP, rather than actually assigning costs based on the use of the transmission
system and the customer’s impact on the system, instead exacerbates the reliability issues with the

extension of the CP mechanism.

Senate Bill 6 contemplates non-bypassable charges for transmission, at least in part,
however the only non-bypassable charges would be minimum demand charges for new, large load
entities; there would be no minimum demand charge for those many transmission users that avoid
paying for transmission charges under the current CP mechanism. Moreover, the 20-year sunsetting
of the minimum demand charge for new large loads is also problematic, and is certainly not based
on cost causation principles. When the demand charge ceases, what was previously considered a
new large load, is no longer considered a new large load, and is free to game the 12CP system. The

life of the transmission facilities constructed to serve new large loads and the costs associated with

 these facilities will far exceed the minimum demand payment period of 20 years described in the
PFP. It is unclear what the basis for the 20-year period in the PFP is—but it appears arbitrary; it
is not tied to cost causation. The PFP also allows other large loads that are not “new” large loads,
or loads that are not “large” (e.g. 74.9 MW and below), whether existing or new loads, to continue
to game the system. The result is discrimination against the smallest customer classes, which must
pick up the slack for all customers that avoid transmission costs today regardless of size, by loads
that are‘not large enough to be required to pay a minimum demand charge, or that existed prior to
the requirement to pay a minimum demand charge. It also discriminates against the new large loads
that may be in the same industry and of the same size as an existing load that is free to fully exploit
the system. Whether due to existing customers that are gaming the system, or new loads that game
the system but are not quite 75 MW so are not considered “large”, or large loads that avoid the
portion of transmission costs associated with the portion of 12CP allocation they are given, the
methodology in the PFP discriminates against smaller customers. SB 6 intended these subsidies to
be removed, and a fair allocation of costs across the board. The PFP does-not change the fact that

smaller customers will continue to subsidize transmission costs for larger customers.

All parties recognize that this project is a zero-sum game. All transmission costs must be
paid to each utility; it is just a matter of who pays. And for many years the “who pays” has been
discriminatory. The “who pays” has been the customers least able to game the system—residential
and small commercial customers. Smaller loads are being charged more for transmission service
than the postage stamp while larger loads pay less than the postage stamp because of the CPs, and

flawed cost of service assumptions. Under the PFP, that does not change. °

Given the unprecedented investments approved by the Legislature and the Commission for
new transmission build-outs, if the transmission cost recovery methodology is not modified to
remove the gaming component, costs for transmission will continue to increase, eventually
approaching the generation cost of the customer’s bill, and will make electric bills unaffordable for
Texans within the Electric Reliability Council of Texas, Inc. ((ERCOT”) footprint. The incentive
to non-residential and larger commercial and industrial loads and now the new large loads, to shift
costs to those consumers that cannot play the CP game, will materially inctease in the future given
the sizable investments occurring and planned for new transmission. Cost causation principles
require that costs be allocated to those that use and benefit from the grid in any and all intervals.

Cost causation principles require that all loads, whether existing or new, or new large loads, that

 benefit from these buildouts bear the costs for the Permian Basin Reliability Plan, the 765 kV STEP
Eastern Backbone, future transmission system investments, and their sharé of overall transmission

costs for use of the system in all hours, not 30-minute intervals occurring once per month.

H-E-B and STEC do not believe that seeking to have smaller customers also game the
system will result in a level playing field. Such a result also would not.be consistent with cost
causation principles and may result in more sophisticated residential customers shifting their costs

onto less sophisticated residential customers.

H-E-B and STEC support a Non-Coincident Peak (“NCP”) transmission cost recovery
mechanism that is a 12 NCP mechanism. It cannot be gamed. It is based on use of the transmission
system at any time. If transmission has been built for a new large load based on their stated demand
and they do not consume the electricity built to serve them, contracted peak demand should be used.
Consistent with cost causation principles, the higher of NCP or contracted-peak demand should be
allocated to new large loads. All other loads should be responsible for their NCP, which represents

their use of the system in any and all intervals.

In Project No. 58484, H-E-B, STEC and a number of parties proposed using an unavoidable
metric, NCP, for all customers that is tied to the customer’s use of the transmission system, and
applicable to all classes such that it is non-discriminatory. The nature of NCP is that it reflects the

actual use of the system, and it cannot be gamed.

II. RESPONSES TO QUESTIONS

1. Should the values associated with the large load minimum billing demand provisions be
different for large load customers with different contracted peak demands or different

non-coincident (NCP) demands?

All loads, new large loads, existing larger loads having a demand either above or below
75 MW, commercial and residential customers should pay NCP. However, if a new large load has
a higher contracted peak demand for which ERCOT and the PUCT have approved that transmission
be built, the new large load should pay “the greater of its NCP or contracted peak demand.”

2. Should the large load minimum billing demand be:
a. fixed for 20 years as proposed;
b. reduced in phases over a period of 20 years; or

c. extended to a longer time period?

 The large load minimum billing demand should persist for the greater of 20 years or the
life of the facilities. For so long as the facilities are used and useful, the minimum billing demand

should apply.

3. Should the large load minimum billing demand be based on some measure of demand
lower than contracted peak demand and NCP demand? For example, should the large load
minimum billing demand:
No, for the reasons stated above, large load minimum billing demand should be based on
the “higher of” contracted peak demand or NCP.

a. reflect a “ratcheted” demand, wherein the large load minimum billing demand is
some percentage of the customer’s contracted peak demand or maximum NCP
demand in the previous year? If so, should the ratchet percentage decline in

phases over the years, and how?
No, see response above, and additionally ratcheted demands are not cost-based.

b. be based on a “weighted average” minimum billing demand, wherein the large
load minimum billing demand is some weighted average of the large load
customer’s contracted peak demand or highest NCP demand over the previous
year and the large load customer’s 12CP demand? If so, should the percentage
weighting towards contracted peak demand or NCP demand decline in phases

over the years, and how?
No, see response above, and additionally averaging is not cost-based.

4, Should separate rate treatment be applied to a large computational load, defined as an
entity that is subject to §25.194 of this title (relating to Large Load Interconnection
Standards) and in which 50% or greater of the demand at the-site consists of power
electronic based load, specifically computational load, such as data centers and
cryptocurrency mining facilities? Responses to this question should include applicable
legal support or limitations regarding separate rate treatment for large computational

loads.

No, the rate treatment should not change. If the operational characteristics of the
large load require that ERCOT take measures to guard against reliability risks, that should not

impact the rate that the load pays for service. Furthermore, SB6 did not create a distinction

5

 between large loads. The Commission should not exceed the authority granted to it by the

Legislature by discriminating in favor of some large loads at the expense of others.

5. Should the definition for transmission interconnection costs be broadened to include
transmission projects that are recommended at the conclusion of a batch study to serve

the transmission capacity needs of a particular load?

Yes, the costs of these projects are part of the costs to interconnect new large loads.
These costs should also be applied to other large loads that are benefiting from the transmission
buildout, whether they are new or existing large loads and whether or not they are defined as large
loads meeting the 75 MW threshold. Other customers should be held harmless from the costs to

serve large loads.

6. Ifa large load customer is able to reserve transmission capacity irrespective of whether
the large load customer has energized or is fully using available capacity, how should
these loads be reflected in the resource adequacy reports and assessments and

transmission planning studies?

This question is not appropriate to a cost causation analysis for transmission cost
allocation, but would be more properly considered in the Large Load Interconnection Standards

rulemaking.
UL. __CONCLUSION

H-E-B and STEC believe that it is critical to address the subsidization issues in
transmission cost allocation prior to utility rates being increased for the many transmission
buildouts in progress, including the Permian Basin Reliability Plan with 765kV lines, the 765kV
STEP Eastern Backbone buildout and the other transmission being built to integrate these large
buildouts into the regional transmission network. H-E-B and STEC seek to have the rule
conform with the SB6 language, therefore cost causation must be the driving factor behind
transmission cost allocation, rather than a sophisticated customer’s success in avoiding costs for

the transmission it utilizes on a daily basis.

 Respectfully submitted,

Diana M. Liebmann

 Executive Summary of H-E-B LP, and South Texas Electric Cooperative, Inc. Joint Comments on
Proposal for Publication in Evaluation of Transmission Cost Recovery Project No. 58000

¢ The Proposal for Publication does not meet the SB 6 requirement to allocate costs based
on cost causation. A CP methodology results in charges based on which customers are
better able to avoid the CP, not on the costs caused by, or the benefits received from, the
transmission system.

¢ ANon-Coincident Peak or NCP mechanism accurately tracks the use of the transmission
system by all customers and cannot be gamed. The Commission should utilize an NCP
mechanism for all loads. ;

¢ New large loads that have contracted peak demands that they do not meet should be
allocated the costs associated with the higher of their NCP or their contracted peak
demand.

e Allocating transmission costs to new large loads without correcting the cost-shifting by
existing loads that avoid the CP intervals, whether under a 4CP methodology or a 12CP
methodology, and whether the duration is 15-minutes or 30-minutes, leaves in place
subsidization of larger loads by smaller customer.

¢ Anew large load minimum demand charge should not end at 20 years. 20 years is
unlikely to be the end of the life of the facilities built for the new large load. The 20-year
cutoff appears to be an arbitrary number, not tied to cost causation.

© The large load minimum demand charge should not be reduced, ratcheted down or part of
a weighted average—it should be directly assigned to the large load. There is no cost
causation reason to reduce, ratchet down or average the costs assigned to a large load for
facilities built and maintained to serve that large load.

¢ Large computational loads should not have separate rate treatment from other large loads.
SB 6 does not discriminate between new large loads on the basis of the type of load, and
ERCOT has the tools to manage the reliability of the system under the SB 6 framework.

¢ The definition of transmission interconnection costs should be broadened to include costs
for transmission determined through the batch study process that benefits a particular load.
